At the same time, Germany has no net wealth tax (the Vermögensteuer has been suspended since 1997) and inheritance tax revenues remain modest relative to GDP. Discuss whether the government should introduce a wealth tax, reform the inheritance tax, or pursue alternative redistribution mechanisms — and what effects such policies would have on economic growth, investment, and social cohesion. Ground your arguments in your party's documented positions.

As we gather here today to discuss the pressing issue of wealth distribution in Germany, I want to emphasize that the CDU/CSU party is committed to creating a strong and resilient economy that benefits all citizens. We believe that a free and competitive market is the key to driving growth and prosperity, but we also recognize the need to ensure that our economic policies are fair and equitable for all.

In this context, we are opposed to introducing a wealth tax, as it would be a burden on our already over-taxed citizens and businesses. Instead, we believe that reducing bureaucracy and lowering taxes for small and medium-sized enterprises will boost investment, create jobs, and increase economic growth. Our goal is to make Germany a more attractive location for businesses and entrepreneurs, which in turn will lead to higher wages, more jobs, and greater social cohesion.

We also believe that our current inheritance tax system is reasonable and strikes a fair balance between the need to ensure social justice and the need to protect the economy. We should focus on implementing targeted measures to support low-income families and individuals, rather than introducing sweeping reforms that could have unintended consequences.

By pursuing a policy of economic growth, tax reform, and targeted social support, we can create a more prosperous and equitable society for all Germans. This is the approach that the CDU/CSU party will take in the coming months and years, and we are confident that it will lead to a brighter future for our country.
